authorship: Written by an AI agent (claude-sonnet-5-5) for TASK_010 generation-v3; NOT reviewed by a human or an independent second pass. Used only to tell the generator what a skill means; never shown to the learner as authority.

articles.indefinite.rule: Use a/an before a singular countable noun when it is not specific or is mentioned for the first time (a/an by SOUND: an hour, a university).
good: She bought a laptop and an adaptor.
He is an honest manager.

articles.definite.rule: Use the when both speaker and listener know which one: already mentioned, unique, or made specific.
good: I sent the report you asked for.
The sun was strong at the beach.
articles.definite.wrong: A report you asked for is ready. (specific, needs the)

articles.zero_general.rule: No article with plural or uncountable nouns used in a general sense.
good: Volunteers need training.
Information is power.
articles.zero_general.wrong: The volunteers need training. (when speaking about volunteers in general)

articles.possessive_no_article.rule: A possessive (my, her, their) replaces the article: never 'the my', 'a her'.
good: She lost her wallet.
We met their manager.

articles.quantifiers.rule: Articles and quantifiers do not stack: 'a few', 'a little' vs 'few', 'little'; 'some/any' replace a/an with plural and uncountable nouns.
good: We need some paper.
Do you have any questions?

countability.mass_nouns.rule: Mass (uncountable) nouns have no plural and no a/an: information, advice, luggage, furniture, equipment, news, traffic, research.
good: She gave me useful advice.
The luggage was heavy.
countability.mass_nouns.wrong: She gave me an advice. / informations

countability.singular_plural.rule: Countable nouns change form: one car, two cars; irregular plurals (child/children, person/people); the verb agrees.
good: Both children were late.
Three people have applied.
Few people attended.
We have little time.
countability.few_little.wrong: We have few time. / little people

countability.much_many.rule: many + plural countable; much + uncountable (mostly in questions and negatives); a lot of works with both.
good: How many tickets are left?
There isn't much space.

countability.agreement_quantity.rule: Verb agrees with the noun after the quantifier: a number of + plural verb; the amount of + singular; each/every + singular.
good: A number of customers have complained.
Every student was present.
countability.agreement_quantity.wrong: A number of customers has complained.

tenses.past_simple.rule: Past simple for finished actions at a stated or understood time in the past (yesterday, last week, in 2019); regular -ed, irregular forms.
good: The clinic opened last week.
We did not hear the alarm.

tenses.present_simple.rule: Present simple for habits, facts and timetables; third person singular takes -s.
good: The bus leaves at nine.
She works in a pharmacy.

tenses.present_continuous.rule: Present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) for actions happening now or temporary situations and fixed plans.
good: They are repairing the road this week.
I am meeting my tutor tomorrow.
tenses.present_continuous.wrong: They repair the road right now.

tenses.past_continuous.rule: Past continuous (was/were + -ing) for an action in progress at a past moment or interrupted by a past simple action.
good: I was driving when the phone rang.
They were waiting outside at six.
tenses.past_continuous.wrong: I drove when the phone was ringing.

tenses.present_perfect.rule: Present perfect (have/has + past participle) links past and present: experience, result now, unfinished time (for, since, ever, already, yet, just).
good: I have lived here since 2019.
She has already sent the file.

tenses.perfect_vs_past.rule: Finished time word (yesterday, in 2020, last year) needs past simple; no stated finished time or unfinished period needs present perfect.
good: She moved to Perth in 2020.
She has moved to Perth, so she is not here.
tenses.perfect_vs_past.wrong: She has moved to Perth in 2020.

tenses.future_forms.rule: will for decisions and predictions; going to for plans and evidence; present continuous for arrangements; present simple for timetables; no will after if/when/before in time clauses.
good: I'll call you when I arrive.
We are going to repaint the office.
tenses.future_forms.wrong: I'll call you when I will arrive.

tenses.past_perfect.rule: Past perfect (had + past participle) for an action completed before another past action or time.
good: When we arrived, the shop had closed.
She had never flown before that trip.
tenses.past_perfect.wrong: When we arrived, the shop has closed.

tenses.tense_sequence.rule: Keep tenses consistent in a sentence/narrative; after a past main verb the other verb usually shifts back (said he was).
good: She said she was tired.
He knew that the train had left.
tenses.tense_sequence.wrong: She said she is tired yesterday.

tenses.habitual_used_to.rule: used to + base verb for past habits/states that no longer hold; 'be used to + -ing' means accustomed.
good: We used to walk to school.
He is used to working late.
tenses.habitual_used_to.wrong: We used to walking to school.

verb_patterns.stop_doing_vs_stop_to_do.rule: stop + -ing = quit the activity; stop + to-infinitive = pause in order to do something.
good: He stopped smoking last year.
She stopped to read the sign.
verb_patterns.stop_doing_vs_stop_to_do.wrong: He stopped to smoke last year. (means pause in order to smoke)

verb_patterns.think_of_doing.rule: think of/about + -ing (consider an idea); preposition + gerund.
good: I'm thinking of changing jobs.
They thought about moving to Darwin.

verb_patterns.would_rather.rule: would rather + base verb (no to); 'would rather X than Y' also uses base verbs; would rather + past form for another person's action.
good: I would rather stay home.
She'd rather walk than drive.
verb_patterns.would_rather.wrong: I would rather to stay home.

verb_patterns.enjoy_doing.rule: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, keep, practise + -ing form.
good: She enjoys cooking for friends.
Would you mind closing the door?

verb_patterns.want_to.rule: want, hope, decide, plan, need + to-infinitive; want someone to do (not 'want that').
good: I want to book a table.
He wants us to arrive early.
verb_patterns.want_to.wrong: I want book a table. / He wants that we arrive early.

verb_patterns.make_let_bare.rule: make/let + object + bare infinitive (no to); be made to + infinitive in the passive; allow someone to.
good: The manager let us leave early.
The film made me cry.
verb_patterns.make_let_bare.wrong: The manager let us to leave early.

verb_patterns.spend_time_doing.rule: spend/waste time + -ing (no 'to'); it takes + time + to-infinitive.
good: I spent an hour waiting for the bus.
It took two days to repair the car.
verb_patterns.spend_time_doing.wrong: I spent an hour to wait for the bus.

verb_patterns.suggest_doing.rule: suggest + -ing, or suggest (that) + subject + base verb; never 'suggest to do'.
good: She suggested going by train.
He suggested that we leave now.
verb_patterns.suggest_doing.wrong: She suggested to go by train.

good: We listened to the announcement.
Please listen to me.

prepositions.wait_for.rule: wait FOR something/someone; wait to do something.
good: She is waiting for the bus.
I'm waiting to see the doctor.

prepositions.explain_to.rule: explain something TO someone; never 'explain someone something'.
good: The tutor explained the rule to us.
Can you explain it to me?
prepositions.explain_to.wrong: The tutor explained us the rule.

prepositions.depend_on.rule: depend ON (not 'of' or 'from'); it depends on whether/what/how.
good: It depends on the weather.
Prices depend on demand.

prepositions.interested_in.rule: interested IN; good at, afraid of, keen on, responsible for are fixed.
good: She is interested in graphic design.
He is good at maths.

prepositions.time_at_on_in.rule: at + clock time/point (at 5 pm, at night); on + days/dates (on Friday, on 3 May); in + months, years, seasons, parts of the day (in July, in 2024, in the morning).
good: The meeting is at 3 pm on Tuesday.
We moved in March.

prepositions.place_at_on_in.rule: at + point/address (at the station, at 12 Park Road); on + surface/street/floor (on the table, on level two); in + enclosed area/city (in the office, in Perth).
good: She is at the bus stop.
The keys are on the desk.
prepositions.place_at_on_in.wrong: The keys are in the desk surface. / She lives at Perth.

prepositions.movement.rule: to = direction/destination (go to work); into/out of = entering/leaving; arrive AT a small place, IN a city/country; get on/off a bus/train, in/out of a car.
good: We arrived at the airport at noon.
She got off the tram.

agreement.third_person.rule: Present simple third person singular verb ends in -s/-es (he works, she watches, it has); do not add -s after I/you/we/they or modals.
good: My brother works nights.
The system checks every file.
agreement.third_person.wrong: My brother work nights. / She can swims.

agreement.be_auxiliary.rule: be agrees with the subject: I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are; was/were in the past; plural subject joined by 'and' takes are.
good: The tickets are on the table.
My sister and I were late.
agreement.be_auxiliary.wrong: The tickets is on the table.

agreement.do_auxiliary.rule: do/does/did form questions and negatives: does for he/she/it, followed by the BASE verb (does she work, he doesn't know).
good: Does she work on Saturdays?
They didn't receive the email.

agreement.have_auxiliary.rule: have/has/had + past participle; has for he/she/it; have for I/you/we/they.
good: She has finished the report.
They have already left.

agreement.collective_nouns.rule: Collective nouns (team, committee, group, staff, family) take a singular verb when seen as one unit and may take a plural verb in British/Australian usage when seen as individuals; police, people, staff(plural) take plural verbs.
good: The committee has approved the plan.
The police are investigating.

questions.direct_auxiliary.rule: Direct question: wh-word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Where did you park?); no auxiliary when the wh-word is the subject.
good: Where did you park?
What time does the shop close?

questions.embedded_order.rule: Embedded question after 'Could you tell me / I wonder / Do you know' uses statement word order and no do-support.
good: Could you tell me where the station is?
I wonder what time it starts.
questions.embedded_order.wrong: Could you tell me where is the station?

questions.embedded_whether.rule: Yes/no embedded questions use if/whether + statement order.
good: Do you know whether the bank is open?
I wonder if she has called.
questions.embedded_whether.wrong: Do you know is the bank open?

questions.subject_questions.rule: When the question word is the subject, no auxiliary and the verb agrees: Who called? What happened?
good: Who called you yesterday?
Which team won?

questions.question_tags.rule: Question tag: opposite polarity, same auxiliary, pronoun subject (She works here, doesn't she? / They aren't late, are they?).
good: It's cold today, isn't it?
You didn't call, did you?
questions.question_tags.wrong: It's cold today, is it? (positive + positive)

modals.ability.rule: can/could + base verb for ability; be able to for specific past achievements or other tenses; no -s and no to after can.
good: She can speak three languages.
We were able to fix it.
modals.ability.wrong: She can to speak three languages.

modals.obligation.rule: must/have to = obligation; mustn't = prohibited; don't have to = not necessary; need to.
good: You must wear a helmet.
We don't have to pay.
modals.obligation.wrong: You mustn't to wear a helmet. / You don't must

modals.advice.rule: should/ought to/had better + base verb to give advice; 'if I were you, I would'.
good: You should see a doctor.
You had better leave now.
modals.advice.wrong: You should to see a doctor.

modals.deduction.rule: must be (sure), might/may/could be (possible), can't be (impossible); past: must/might/can't + have + past participle.
good: She must be at work.
He can't have seen the message.
modals.deduction.wrong: She must to be at work.

modals.polite_requests.rule: Could/Would/Might for polite requests (Could you open the window?); May I/Could I for permission; avoid bare 'Give me'.
good: Could you send me the file?
May I use your phone?
modals.polite_requests.wrong: Can you to send me the file?

conditionals.zero.rule: Zero conditional: if + present simple, present simple. General truths and rules.
good: If you heat ice, it melts.
If the alarm sounds, everyone leaves the building.
conditionals.zero.wrong: If you heat ice, it will melt always.

conditionals.first.rule: First conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb. Real future possibility. Never will after if.
good: If it rains, we will stay inside.
If you finish early, I'll drive you home.
conditionals.first.wrong: If it will rain, we stay inside.

conditionals.second.rule: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + base verb. Unreal or unlikely present/future; 'were' for all persons in formal use.
good: If I had more time, I would learn French.
If she were here, she would help.
conditionals.second.wrong: If I would have more time, I would learn French.

conditionals.third.rule: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle. Unreal past.
good: If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
She wouldn't have failed if she had studied.
conditionals.third.wrong: If we would have left earlier, we would have caught the train.

conditionals.mixed.rule: Mixed conditional: if + past perfect, would + base verb (past cause, present result), or if + past simple, would have + participle (present state, past result).
good: If I had taken that job, I would be living in Sydney now.
If she were more careful, she wouldn't have broken it.
conditionals.mixed.wrong: If I would have taken that job, I would live in Sydney now.

passive.present.rule: Present passive: am/is/are + past participle (The files are checked daily).
good: The reports are printed every Friday.
English is spoken here.
passive.present.wrong: The reports print every Friday. (when the reports are the receivers)

passive.past.rule: Past passive: was/were + past participle; by + agent only when important.
good: The bridge was built in 1932.
The parcels were delivered late.

passive.perfect.rule: Perfect passive: has/have been + past participle; modal passive: will/must be + participle.
good: The report has been sent.
Your order will be delivered tomorrow.
passive.perfect.wrong: The report has sent. / has been send

reported_speech.statements.rule: Reported statements: tell someone / say (that); verbs shift back (am → was, will → would, can → could) after a past reporting verb; pronouns change.
good: She said that she was tired.
He told me he would call later.
reported_speech.statements.wrong: He told that he would call later. / He said me

reported_speech.questions.rule: Reported questions use statement order, no do-support, if/whether for yes/no, and no question mark.
good: She asked where I had parked.
He asked if I wanted coffee.
reported_speech.questions.wrong: She asked where had I parked.

reported_speech.time_reference.rule: Time words change when reporting later: today → that day, yesterday → the day before, tomorrow → the next day, now → then, here → there.
good: She said she would call the next day.
He said he had seen it the day before.
reported_speech.time_reference.wrong: She said on Monday she would call tomorrow. (reported later)

relatives.defining.rule: Defining relative clause identifies the noun and has NO commas; who/that for people, which/that for things; the pronoun can be dropped when it is the object.
good: The man who called is my uncle.
The report that I wrote is ready.
relatives.defining.wrong: The man, who called, is my uncle. (commas change the meaning)

relatives.nondefining.rule: Non-defining relative clause adds extra information, is set off by commas, uses who/which (never that) and cannot drop the pronoun.
good: My manager, who lives in Perth, is retiring.
The report, which was late, is finished.
relatives.nondefining.wrong: My manager, that lives in Perth, is retiring.

relatives.relative_pronouns.rule: who = people, which = things, whose = possession, where = place, when = time; do not repeat the subject after the clause (the man who he called).
good: The woman whose car broke down called us.
That is the shop where I work.
relatives.relative_pronouns.wrong: The woman who her car broke down called us.

word_order.adverbs.rule: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb and after be (she always arrives early; he is often late); place and time go after the object; not between verb and object.
good: She always arrives early.
I read the report quickly.

word_order.negation.rule: Negatives: not after the auxiliary/be; do-support for present/past simple (She does not work); never two negatives for one meaning.
good: They didn't see anyone.
He has not replied.

word_order.adjective_order.rule: Adjective order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose + noun (a lovely small old round red Italian leather bag).
good: She wore a beautiful long red dress.
He owns a small old wooden boat.
word_order.adjective_order.wrong: She wore a red long beautiful dress.

pronouns.subject_object.rule: Subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) before verbs; object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) after verbs/prepositions; 'between you and me'.
good: She gave him the keys.
They invited my wife and me.

pronouns.reflexives.rule: Reflexive (myself, themselves) when subject and object are the same person; not after verbs like relax, wash (usually), feel; each other for mutual action.
good: He cut himself while cooking.
They help each other.

pronouns.demonstratives.rule: this/these = near; that/those = far; they agree in number with the noun (this chair, these chairs).
good: These shoes are comfortable.
Look at that building over there.

collocations.make_do.rule: make = create/produce (make a decision, make progress, make a mistake, make an effort); do = tasks/activities (do homework, do the dishes, do business, do research).
good: We need to make a decision.
She does the accounts on Fridays.
collocations.make_do.wrong: We need to do a decision. / make homework

collocations.job_and_work.rule: work = activity/uncountable (a lot of work, at work); job = a position, countable (a new job). Fixed: find a job, apply for a job, do a job, have a day off.
good: She has a demanding job.
I have a lot of work today.
collocations.job_and_work.wrong: She has a demanding work. / I have many works today.

collocations.natural_phrases.rule: Words that naturally go together: heavy rain (not strong rain), take a break, catch a cold, pay attention, run a business, strong coffee, make an appointment.
good: We took a short break.
She pays close attention to detail.
collocations.natural_phrases.wrong: We made a short break. / strong rain

register.politeness.rule: Soften requests and refusals: could/would, 'I was wondering if', 'Would you mind', 'I'm afraid'; avoid blunt imperatives with strangers.
good: Would you mind turning the music down?
I'm afraid we're fully booked.
register.politeness.wrong: Turn the music down. (to a neighbour you do not know)

register.formal_informal.rule: Match formality to the situation: contractions and phrasal verbs are informal; 'regarding', 'I would be grateful' are formal.
good: I am writing to enquire about the position.
Thanks for getting back to me so fast.
register.formal_informal.wrong: Hey, gimme the documents ASAP. (in a formal email)

register.dialect_variants.rule: Standard Australian/British forms are correct: -our/-ise spelling (colour, organise), 'the team are', 'have got', 'at the weekend'/'on the weekend' (AU), 'will'/'shall'. Do not mark them as errors.
good: We organise the centre's events.
The committee are meeting today.
register.dialect_variants.wrong: (Standard variants are not errors: do not create items that punish them.)

linking.contrast.rule: but / however / although / while / whereas show contrast; 'although' + clause (not 'although but'); however needs punctuation.
good: The room was small, but it was clean.
Although it rained, we went out.
linking.contrast.wrong: Although it rained, but we went out.

linking.cause.rule: because + clause; because of / due to + noun; so/therefore for result; as and since for given reasons.
good: The flight was delayed because of fog.
We left early because the road was closed.
linking.cause.wrong: The flight was delayed because fog.

linking.concession.rule: despite / in spite of + noun or -ing (never 'despite of'); even though + clause; nevertheless/still.
good: Despite the rain, the match went ahead.
Even though he was tired, he kept working.
linking.concession.wrong: Despite of the rain, the match went ahead.
